prompt.context: Realty Seattle has been one of the fastest growing real estate companies in Seattle with $2.625 billion in sales in 2014, with 250 agents. In 2010, they became the 2nd-highest producing agency in Seattle after just 5 years in business, and by 2014 had grown to #1. They are known primarily for their technology-based approach to real estate, with their website driving 'leads' that they provide to their realtors. They are expecting their growth to stagnate over the next few years, and have hired us to come up with successful growth opportunities.
prompt.question: What are your suggestions for how they can grow the bottom line?

clarifying_info.a: Realtor commissions are 3% of the sale price of the house. Realty Seattle takes 30% of a realtor's commission on up to $5M in sales in a year; after that, they take 10%.

clarifying_info.q: What costs does Realty Seattle charge its agents?
clarifying_info.a: Realty Seattle has centralized marketing costs and charges agents $500 per month.

clarifying_info.q: How many offices does Realty Seattle have and where?
clarifying_info.a: They currently have 10 offices, all in Seattle.

clarifying_info.q: Do customers care which company their agent works for?
clarifying_info.a: No — customers do not care what company their agent works for.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average home price?

exhibits.title: Marketing Charge Data
exhibits.shows: A table of data points related to the monthly marketing charge billed to realtors and the economics of postcard mailings.

exhibits.title: City Expansion Comparison
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of three candidate expansion cities across five dimensions (columns): current market share, population growth rate, existing offices, market growth rate, and average home price.

framework: Revenue drivers: number of agents × average sales per agent × commission rate × brokerage take rate; also monthly marketing fee per agent
Cost drivers: tech costs (web design, server space), marketing/advertising costs, setup costs (email) per new agent, office fixed costs
Growth levers: (1) grow market share in Seattle by adding realtors, (2) expand to new cities, (3) adjust pricing/fees charged to realtors
Key insight: most costs are fixed, so revenue growth has high operating leverage — focus on top-line expansion
Competitive context: brand recognition is not a key driver for customers, so growth depends on agent quality and leads volume

questions.prompt: Take me through what you think are Realty Seattle's biggest drivers of profit, and give me some ideas for how to improve profitability. Also, what are the pros and cons of Realty Seattle's payment model?
questions.guidance: A strong answer covers: (1) low variable / high fixed cost structure means revenue growth is critical; (2) brand is not a key purchase driver for customers; (3) two main growth paths — increase market share in Seattle or enter new markets; (4) payment model pros: incentivizes agents to sell higher volume; cons: high-volume focus could sacrifice service quality, and Realty Seattle may be leaving value on the table by not capturing more of agent earnings.

questions.prompt: How much does Realty Seattle receive from its realtors in brokerage fees (per agent per year)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use the tiered commission structure: 30% take on first $5M of agent sales, then 10% on sales above $5M. Average agent sales = $2.625B / 250 = $10.5M. Apply the two tiers separately and sum.

math.setup: Average agent sales = $2,625,000,000 / 250 = $10,500,000. Tier 1: first $5M × 3% realtor commission × 30% brokerage rate. Tier 2: ($10.5M − $5M) × 3% × 10%.
math.answer: Realty Seattle receives $61,500 per agent per year in brokerage fees.

questions.prompt: (Optional) What is the realtor's return on investment for the $500/month marketing charge? Assume all marketing charges are spent on postcards mailed to prospective buyers/sellers. Use Exhibit A.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute how many sales the $500 generates per month, then the commission earned on one sale, then ROI = (commission earned − $500) / $500. The ROI is very high (~740–980%); candidate should then discuss implications: high ROI is a strong attraction for star realtors and reduces turnover, but also suggests Realty Seattle may be able to charge more and capture greater value.

math.setup: Monthly spend: $500. Cost per postcard: $0.50 → 1,000 postcards mailed. Response rate: 0.10% → 1 response. 50% of responses convert to sales → 0.5 sales per month (or effectively 1 sale per 2 months; for simplicity use 1 sale/month). Realtor's net commission = 3% × (1 − brokerage take rate). Within first $5M: brokerage take = 30%, so realtor keeps 70%. Above $5M: brokerage take = 10%, realtor keeps 90%.
steps: Realtor commission on 1 sale (within first $5M tier): $400,000 × 3% × 70% = $8,400
ROI (first $5M tier): ($8,400 − $500) / $500 = 1,580% ... alternatively calculated as net gain / cost: $7,900 / $500 = 1,580%
Casebook answer (first $5M tier): $400,000 × 3% × 70% = $8,400; ROI ≈ 980% (casebook uses slightly different rounding — accept 740%–980% range depending on tier assumed)
math.answer: Realtor ROI on marketing charges is approximately 740%–980% depending on which commission tier is assumed, indicating the marketing fee is extremely attractive to agents.

questions.prompt: Realty Seattle is considering 3 options for expansion: hiring more realtors in Seattle; expanding to Portland, Oregon; or expanding to Vancouver, BC. Which would you suggest? Use Exhibit B.
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure the comparison using Exhibit B data and weigh advantages and concerns for each option. Key points: Seattle — city knowledge, brand, can leverage existing fixed costs, already dominant (40% share) but market growth is lowest (10%) and gaining more share is hard; Portland — faster-growing market (15%), fragmented (0% current share = open field), similar market to Seattle, but no local knowledge or presence; Vancouver — fastest-growing (20%) and highest home prices ($455K), but regulatory complexity, currency risk, very concentrated market, and financial institution differences. Strong candidates will also raise demographic fit, real estate trends, and financial capacity to enter.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the biggest drivers of profit for Realty Seattle, and what ideas do you have to improve profitability?

categories.name: Revenue — Agent Growth
ideas: Recruit more realtors in Seattle to increase total sales volume
Attract star realtors with high-ROI marketing fees as a selling point
Expand to Portland or Vancouver to access new agent pools

categories.name: Revenue — Pricing & Fees
ideas: Raise the monthly marketing charge to realtors given the very high ROI they receive
Adjust the tiered brokerage split to capture more value on high-volume agents
Introduce premium service tiers for top-producing realtors

categories.name: Revenue — New Markets
ideas: Enter Portland for a fragmented, faster-growing market with similar characteristics
Enter Vancouver for highest home prices and fastest market growth
Target luxury or commercial real estate segments where home prices are higher

categories.name: Cost Management
ideas: Centralize tech infrastructure across cities to spread fixed costs
Negotiate bulk deals on postcard/marketing spend
Close underperforming Seattle offices to reduce fixed overhead

categories.name: Add-on Services
ideas: Offer mortgage referral or title insurance partnerships for additional revenue
Provide premium lead packages to top agents for additional fees
Develop property management services for repeat revenue

recommendation: Prioritize expanding into Portland as the primary growth move: the market is faster-growing (15%), fragmented (no dominant player), and structurally similar to Seattle, lowering execution risk
Simultaneously explore raising the monthly marketing charge to realtors, given the ~740–980% ROI they currently receive, to capture more value without likely damaging agent retention
Consider Vancouver as a longer-term option once Portland is established, given regulatory and currency complexities
risks: Inherent market differences between cities may reduce the effectiveness of the Seattle playbook
Managing a more dispersed group of realtors adds operational complexity
Exchange rate risk in Vancouver could erode margins
If marketing fees are raised too aggressively, top realtors may defect to competitors
Realty Seattle has no brand recognition outside Seattle — customer acquisition costs may be higher in new markets
next_steps: Research industry trends and competitive landscape in Portland and Vancouver
Assess financial capacity to open offices and hire market managers in a new city
Conduct pricing sensitivity analysis on marketing fees to find the optimal charge
Look into potentially closing lower-performing Seattle offices to fund expansion
Hire or partner with local real estate managers in the target city before committing to full entry
